records.name: Cell lineage, identity and state
records.tldr: A cell’s ancestry, its type and its current activity answer different questions. Similar activity does not prove that two cells share a recent ancestor.
records.summary: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

Weinreb and colleagues combined expressed barcodes and transcriptomes over time in hematopoiesis; sister-cell analyses exposed fate biases that a single RNA snapshot missed. This does not identify an individual tumor’s origin from its expression profile.

Lim and colleagues studied normal and preneoplastic breast tissue from BRCA1 mutation carriers and found an expanded luminal-progenitor population. The expression profiles of BRCA1-associated tissue and basal breast tumours resembled normal luminal progenitors more than the other tested subsets. This supported a candidate population for transformation; it was not direct lineage tracing of an individual tumour. A luminal-progenitor-like RNA program does not by itself make a cancer hormone-receptor-positive.

Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

In a fictional set with separately established shared genetic ancestry, one cell is cycling and another is noncycling. Different activity labels do not require different ancestry. Conversely, two cells in the same RNA cluster need not belong to the same genetic clone. The origin of the ancestry label matters: expression resemblance alone does not establish it.

records.name: Epithelium, stroma and tissue compartments
records.tldr: Tissue contains different cell groups and supporting material. Knowing which compartment produced a signal helps explain what the result can mean.
records.summary: Epithelium forms linings, coverings and glands; an epithelial cell is not necessarily malignant. A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath an epithelium, distinct from each cell’s lipid membrane. Stroma includes supporting cells, extracellular matrix and vascular structures, rather than only collagen or fibroblasts. Immune cells and other nonmalignant cells can contribute to a tumor specimen. The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.

notes: Bulk RNA or protein measurements combine contributions from sampled cells. A stronger signal can reflect more cells of one type, changed expression within cells, or both. Spatial review and suitable cell markers help test attribution; a mixed-tissue result should not automatically be assigned to cancer cells. Normal and cancer breast atlases provide defined examples of this cellular diversity.

An epithelial marker helps identify a cell compartment; a positive lineage stain alone does not establish malignancy or invasion. Tissue architecture matters. For an epithelial carcinoma, assessing in-situ versus invasive disease includes microscopic review of the basement membrane and surrounding tissue. The SEER summary-stage manual retains site-specific exceptions; this boundary is not a universal staging rule for every cancer.

In a fictional comparison, gene R is high in cancer cells, low in fibroblasts and similarly high in normal luminal epithelial cells. The first contrast supports higher expression than fibroblasts, even if it passes a statistical threshold; it does not establish cancer selectivity. The normal epithelial comparison addresses that claim more closely, while leaving other organs, cell states and target accessibility untested. If that reference group is tiny, contaminated or prepared differently, preserve the unresolved comparison rather than declaring selectivity or exact equality. Normal epithelial cells can also contribute familiar lineage markers to a tumour specimen. An image-based tumour mask is an assignment that needs validation for its actual method and specimens, rather than automatic proof that every included cell is malignant.

records.name: Alleles, zygosity and copy state
records.tldr: An allele is a sequence version at a genomic location. Which versions are present and how many DNA copies exist are separate questions.
records.summary: At a diploid location, heterozygous means that the two copies differ in the feature being considered; homozygous means they match. Hemizygous describes a single copy in the specified context. Tumor gains, losses and genome doubling can make a two-copy model inadequate. Loss of heterozygosity means loss of previously different allelic information; it can accompany a deletion or occur while total copy count remains unchanged. Total copy number alone cannot identify which allele was retained.

notes: Variant allele frequency counts supporting reads or molecules under the assay’s definition. Purity, local copy state, subclonal mixtures and method affect it; it is not directly a cancer-cell percentage or a zygosity call. Phase asks whether specified variants share a DNA copy, a further question that a gene-name match does not answer.

Biallelic inactivation concerns whether either parental contribution still supplies useful function in the relevant cancer-cell population, rather than simply counting two physical DNA copies or two events somewhere in a tissue. A damaging change plus loss of the other contribution can support it, but phasing, allele-specific copy state, consequence and cell mixture matter. High VAF alone cannot establish this state. Nguyen and colleagues' pan-cancer analysis associated particular biallelic repair-gene alterations with genomic damage patterns; that association does not make every variant in every repair gene functionally equivalent or establish present drug sensitivity.

A haplotype groups linked sequence variants on a chromosome that tend to be inherited together. Phasing assigns variants to chromosome copies; that is different from counting carrier cancer cells. Labels A and B distinguish sequence versions without grading either as harmful or harmless. In a fictional set of 100 cancer cells, two variants each present in forty cells could occupy the same forty or separate groups of forty. The two individual fractions do not reveal their overlap. Joint sequence or cell-resolved evidence addresses co-occurrence, with its own sampling limits. Neither shared prevalence nor physical phase alone establishes a variant's functional importance.

records.name: Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity (gLOH)
records.tldr: This assay-defined score summarizes genomic regions that lost previously different allelic information. It can reflect a past repair defect, including changes that preserve total DNA copy count.
records.summary:
Loss of heterozygosity means loss of previously distinct allelic information at a locus. It can accompany copy loss or occur with a copy-neutral allelic change; tumor purity and ploidy complicate inference. Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity summarizes affected interrogated regions according to the assay’s definition. It is studied as a genomic scar associated with some homologous-recombination-repair defects, rather than a direct measurement of present repair function.

The threshold belongs to the assay and setting. ARIEL2 part 1 prespecified 14 percent or more as LOH high in its ovarian-cancer analysis; this does not establish a universal cutoff. Pan-cancer studies found elevated gLOH associated with biallelic BRCA1/2 alterations and with a core set of other repair-gene alterations, with effects differing by cancer context. Monoallelic calls and an HRR-gene-list label are not interchangeable with those findings. TP53 loss was independently associated with gLOH in the Westphalen analysis.

In 3,476 prostate tumors, Chung and colleagues found BRCA1/2, ATR and FANCA alterations associated with high gLOH, while CDK12-altered tumors, about 6 percent of that cohort, were infrequently gLOH high. The study did not correlate these findings with clinical outcomes. Such associations support gene-specific biological questions; they do not establish an individual patient’s drug benefit or current treatment eligibility.

notes: A scar is different from a present functional defect. gLOH does not by itself establish which repair gene is affected, whether both alleles are inactivated, or whether repair remains impaired. A tumour can retain an earlier genomic scar after its functional state changes.

There is no single gLOH-high cutoff across assays and cancers. ARIEL2 part 1 used a prespecified assay threshold in ovarian carcinoma. Preserve the assay, specimen and reporting context, including uncertainty near a categorical threshold.

Tumour sequencing and clinical hereditary testing answer different questions. The historical TRITON2 study reported similar objective response rates in germline- and somatic-BRCA groups in its enrolled prostate-cancer population; that result is not a current treatment-access rule or evidence that a negative hereditary assay excludes acquired tumour variants.

A local LOH state and a genome-wide LOH score have different scope. In an idealised informative A/B region, 1+1 and 2+0 both total two copies, but only 2+0 loses one sequence version. A total-copy profile alone cannot distinguish them. Allele-aware inputs and purity/ploidy assumptions constrain the call; a genome-wide score does not identify the retained sequence, phase a mutation or directly measure current gene function.

records.name: Copy number alteration (CNA)
records.tldr: A copy number alteration is a stretch of DNA that a tumour has gained extra copies of or lost, from a single gene to a whole chromosome arm.
records.summary: Copy number variation is a form of structural variation in which sections of the genome are duplicated or deleted (Wikipedia); in tumours the acquired form is called a somatic copy number alteration. Arm-level and focal events are called from arrays or sequencing, and GISTIC2.0 is the standard method for finding regions amplified or deleted more often than chance across a cohort. CNA is one of TCGA's core data types and a modality in most multi-omic models.

records.name: Gene amplification and copy-number change
records.tldr: Cancer cells often have extra copies of a growth gene (amplification) or have lost copies of a protective one (deletion), rather than a spelling change within the gene. Extra copies of HER2 or MYCN are classic examples that change treatment.
records.summary: Amplification (detected by FISH, ISH or NGS copy-number calls) can increase gene dosage and expression: HER2 in breast and gastric cancer, MYCN in high-risk neuroblastoma, MET amplification as a resistance route to EGFR inhibitors, CCNE1 in ovarian and gastric cancer, MDM2 in liposarcoma, CDK4 in glioma. Deletions remove tumour suppressors: del(17p)/TP53 in CLL and myeloma (predicting chemo-resistance), CDKN2A/B in glioma (defining grade 4), MTAP (creating a PRMT5 vulnerability), 9p21 loss linked to immunotherapy resistance. Loss of heterozygosity and larger chromosome changes contribute to some method-defined genomic-scar scores. Their clinical interpretation depends on the exact test, cancer and treatment setting; a copy state alone does not establish current repair function or drug benefit.

notes: Total copy count, allele identity, RNA abundance and protein activity are separate measurements. Purity, ploidy and the assay’s definition affect copy calls. Fehrmann and colleagues related copy number to expression after modelling shared transcriptional components in large datasets; that association does not promise a fixed protein increase, target dependence or treatment benefit in a particular tumour.
Total copy number counts copies of a region; allele-specific copy number estimates the contributions of the distinguishable sequence versions A and B.
1+1 is two copies with both versions; 1+0 is one copy with LOH (deletion); 2+0 is copy-neutral LOH (two copies, one version); 2+1 is three copies with both versions retained.
LOH is not synonymous with deletion: copy-neutral LOH can follow loss plus duplication or recombination; a gain does not necessarily erase either version.

Major and minor counts are the larger and smaller allelic contributions; minor of zero supports LOH under the model; they do not identify parental origin or assign a mutation to a copy; phasing needs suitable evidence.
Local copy count differs from ploidy; relative signal can fit different purity and ploidy pairs; fractional counts can reflect mixture or subclonal states.

Methods combine relative coverage with allele balance at informative heterozygous sites, segment the genome and fit states; a matched normal helps; a total-copy profile alone cannot separate 1+1 from 2+0; homozygous sites are uninformative.
Copy state does not establish phase, gene inactivity, expression, dependency or drug response; bulk fits can hide subpopulations and unsampled lesions.
Fictional teaching exercise: Two A copies and no B copies under an adequate model is copy-neutral LOH: not deleted and not proven inactive.

For copy-state analysis, record tumour and suitable normal DNA, extraction consumption, relative depth and informative-site balance, segmentation, total/major/minor copies and purity/ploidy uncertainty. Reanalysis alone needs no tissue. Low purity, uninformative sites and ambiguous fits limit inference; amplification and functional-loss criteria are method-specific.

In a cancer copy-number report, an amplicon is an amplified DNA segment and can contain several genes. TCGA described multiple HER2-amplicon-associated genes, including GRB7, in its breast-cancer analysis. A regional gain does not identify every included gene as a driver or guarantee the same multiplication of RNA or protein; allele-specific state, expression, location and functional importance remain separate questions.

records.name: Tumour purity
records.tldr: Tumour purity is the fraction of cells in a sample that are actually cancer cells rather than normal, immune or stromal cells.
records.summary: Aran, Sirota and Butte's pan-cancer analysis of TCGA estimated the proportion of cancer cells in each sample by several methods (pathologist counts, copy number, expression and methylation based estimators) and showed purity varies widely between and within cancer types and confounds molecular comparisons. Bulk sequencing measures the whole mixture, so a low-purity sample can look like a different tumour; models trained on bulk data inherit this.

notes: Purity estimates and ploidy fits belong to the tested region and method. A pathology estimate of malignant-cell proportion and a sequencing model fit can disagree. Ploidy is a genome-wide average; local copy number can differ. Several purity-ploidy combinations may explain similar data.

Idealised arithmetic assumes diploid normal cells, diploid cancer cells and one mutant copy in every cancer cell: at purity 80%, 50% and 20%, expected variant allele fractions are 40%, 25% and 10%. A one-copy cancer-cell deletion yields mixed average copy numbers 1.2, 1.5 and 1.8 respectively. Copy changes and subclones alter these relationships.

Purity describes the malignant-cell share of the sampled cell mixture; a DNA-based estimate must account for how many genome copies the cells contribute. Ploidy is the average cancer-cell genome copy number. The marble-mixture analogy stops where local copy number and subclonal differences make each cell contribution unequal.

ASCAT reported aneuploidy above 2.7 genome copies in 45% of its early breast cancer series and near-triploid basal-like genomes consistent with loss followed by duplication. A separate advanced-cancer study identified whole-genome doubling in nearly 30% of 9,692 patients. These populations are different. A region with three copies can be a relative loss against a four-copy baseline, while exceeding a normal diploid count.

Nine pathologists estimated tumour-cell content on 47 lung tumour slides; 33% of estimates differed from manually counted content by at least three categories, mostly 10 percentage-points wide. ASCAT and ABSOLUTE jointly infer purity and ploidy from allelic copy number and related signals. Several fits, subclonal changes and low tumour content can complicate interpretation; a model fit is not a direct count.

Copy-number-based genomic scars depend on segmentation and interpretation of purity and ploidy. Popova used ploidy-specific large-scale transition cutoffs in basal-like breast cancers. Telli evaluated a combined loss-of-heterozygosity, telomeric-imbalance and large-scale-transition score of at least 42 or BRCA1/2 mutation in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant TNBC trials. This does not create a universal HRD threshold or prove current repair function or treatment benefit from a fit alone.

Fictional near-diploid example: 18% variant allele fraction is compatible with one mutant copy in every malignant cell at 36% purity, assuming diploid normal cells and no local copy change. It does not prove clonality. At 90% purity, the same VAF would need a different explanation such as subclonality or copy-number context. A negative low-purity result can reflect limited detection, not biological absence.

Sequencing purity belongs to the region used for extraction. Tumour-bed cellularity is an area-based residual cancer burden input, while plasma tumour fraction concerns circulating DNA. Sparse residual malignant cells can make post-treatment sequencing difficult; retain the tested block and laboratory-specific detection limits.

A pathology estimate uses the represented slide region, while a computational purity/ploidy estimate fits sequencing copy-number and allele-fraction data. Fitting those existing data uses no additional tissue. Report purity as a fraction or percentage and ploidy as average cancer-genome copies, such as 2.1 or 3.8, with the region, method and model assumptions.

Laboratories set minimum tumour content for the particular assay. Too few tumour cells, contamination, subclonal copy changes or several similarly good model fits can make the estimate uncertain. Purity and ploidy do not identify which mutations drive the cancer or which treatment will work.

records.name: Cell composition confound (tumour versus stroma and immune cells)
records.tldr: Because a tumour sample is a mix of cancer, stromal and immune cells, a difference between two samples may only reflect a different mix of cells.
records.summary:
A tumour specimen can contain malignant, immune, stromal and normal cells. A difference in an aggregate molecular signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells or both. That is different from a directly counted cell fraction or a density per sampled area, each of which also needs its denominator and sampled region.

Preparation can change what is recovered. Slyper and colleagues compared single-cell and single-nucleus profiling in matched tumour specimens and found similar cell types at sometimes different proportions. A recovered profile mixture is therefore not automatically the original tissue census. Deconvolution and purity models can help investigate contributions under assumptions; they do not certify the cell of origin of every signal or remove sampling differences.

notes: In a fictional assay using equal sampled areas and the same counting method, ten immune cells among fifty total cells is 20%, while ten among twenty is 50%. The immune count remains ten. Loss of other cells can raise the fraction without additional immune-cell entry; these observations alone do not establish recruitment, recognition or killing. This simple cell fraction is not the clinical stromal tumour-infiltrating-lymphocyte score, which has a different denominator.

A second invented comparison starts with ten cells in one square millimetre of viable edge from lesion L. Follow-up A counts ten in the same stated area and region of L, giving ten cells per square millimetre at both times under the supplied assumptions. Follow-up B counts ten in 0.2 square millimetres from an injured centre of lesion M, giving fifty per square millimetre. B does not show a rise within L. Retain the lesion, viable area, centre or edge, collection time, treatment context and counting method. An early sample can capture transient injury signals and a later one a changed surviving-cell mixture. Equal area does not make separate tissue pieces identical, and matched sampling alone still cannot establish recruitment causation.

Measurement layers ask different questions. Anatomical imaging describes structure; tracer imaging depends on the stated product and its distribution; immunohistochemistry localises a protein in sampled tissue; bulk RNA pools captured messages; receptor sequencing describes recovered sequences and their sampled abundances; and controlled recognition or killing assays test a specified function under their conditions. RNA abundance is not accessible surface protein. Formenti's lung-cancer radiation-plus-ipilimumab study used clinical, blood-repertoire and selected functional readouts together; none is a universal immune-success marker or a substitute for the other measurements.

records.name: Myoepithelial cells and the breast basement membrane
records.tldr: Myoepithelial cells are living cells around normal breast ducts and acini; basement membrane is separate extracellular material outside them.
records.summary: These layers help organise normal breast structures and support pathological assessment of invasion. Their location, morphology, staining controls and diagnostic context matter more than a single positive or negative marker.

notes: Typical normal breast ducts and acini have luminal epithelial cells facing the lumen, an outer living myoepithelial layer, extracellular basement membrane and then stroma. Myoepithelial cells have contractile features that help move milk; they are not the chest muscle. Basement membrane contains matrix proteins such as laminins and type IV collagen, not living cells.

Basement membrane beneath an epithelial structure differs from plasma membrane around one cell. Cell polarity describes different inward and outward organisation. Gudjonsson and colleagues' human-cell culture experiments showed that normal myoepithelial cells or laminin-1 could restore luminal orientation in collagen gels; this is model evidence about organisation, not a demonstrated cancer treatment.

Myoepithelial immunohistochemistry is supporting evidence interpreted with morphology. p63 is nuclear; calponin and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain are cytoplasmic markers. Ask which cells stain, where they stain and whether technical controls work. A failed positive control undermines an apparently absent rim.

Werling and colleagues found gaps around some noninvasive structures, stromal staining with muscle-associated markers and p63 staining in some carcinoma cells. Gusterson and colleagues found basement-membrane proteins in some invasive carcinomas. Neither marker absence nor protein presence alone proves the tissue boundary. Basal-like RNA features also do not establish myoepithelial ancestry.

In Gusterson and colleagues' 1982 tissue study, laminin and type IV collagen were detected in normal breast, benign lesions and grade I invasive carcinomas but were absent from grade II and III infiltrating carcinomas in that study. That historical cohort does not make protein presence proof of an intact noninvasive boundary, or protein absence a universal grade rule.

Werling and colleagues examined 85 breast lesions. In that series, at least focal p63 staining in tumour cells occurred in 11% of cases, while stromal myofibroblasts stained with smooth muscle myosin heavy chain in 8% and calponin in 76%. Some noninvasive structures had gaps. These assay- and cohort-specific observations explain why localisation and controls matter; they are not universal diagnostic accuracy estimates.

CAP's morphology-based histological classification and supporting-marker assessment answer a tissue question. A schematic rim is neither an immunostain result nor a diagnosis; illustrated gaps or colours cannot establish invasion. Interpret the actual tissue architecture and appropriately controlled stains together.

records.name: HLA (human leukocyte antigen) and MHC
records.tldr: HLA molecules sit on cells and hold up small pieces of the cell's proteins for T cells to inspect. A T cell reads the fragment together with the particular HLA version holding it.
records.summary:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. records.name: T-cell receptor
records.tldr: A conventional T-cell receptor recognises a peptide together with its HLA display. Recognition alone does not show killing.
records.summary:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

Cross-reactivity is recognition of multiple targets by a receptor. Defined receptor experiments demonstrated peptide/HLA cross-reactivity, not recognition of every allele by an arbitrary receptor or a universal rate. Greater affinity or a contact drawing does not establish healthy-tissue safety.

Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.

Vaccination generally recruits or expands existing mature receptor specificities rather than rewriting each mature receptor. Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. If one beta sequence pairs with different alpha chains, a positive reconstruction of one pair does not establish the other pair's function or tumour killing.

Stone and colleagues review those distinctions, rather than a universal affinity ranking against every antibody. One receptor type per cell is also a simplification: extra productive alpha chains and dual surface receptors have been documented. A chain sequence alone does not establish which assembled receptor provides the measured specificity.

records.name: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs)
records.tldr: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes are lymphocytes found in tumour tissue. Their identity, location, measurement denominator and function answer different questions.
records.summary: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are lymphocytes found in sampled tumour tissue, including T- and B-cell populations. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by a defined mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within eligible tumour-associated stroma on H&E sections. Higher pretreatment scores were associated with better outcomes in the cited early triple-negative breast cancer cohorts, but those associations do not guarantee an individual outcome or establish extra benefit from pembrolizumab. Intratumoral location, stromal area, immune-cell counts and cells expanded for TIL therapy are different measurements or uses.

notes: The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by mononuclear inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and plasma cells, as a percentage of eligible tumour-associated stroma. It is not the percentage of all cells, a CD8-cell count or the fraction of cancer cells being killed.

Define the eligible region and treatment setting before estimating the percentage. Use the specified exclusions for normal structures, in-situ disease, necrosis, crush damage and biopsy-site changes, and assess the region overall rather than only its hottest spot. A prognostic association does not establish added benefit from a particular treatment.

In the pooled analysis of 2,148 early-stage TNBC patients given anthracycline-based chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in pretreatment stromal TILs corresponded to an adjusted invasive disease-free survival hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.91) and overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89). These associations do not establish an added pembrolizumab benefit by TIL level.

Among 906 TNBC patients from six neoadjuvant chemotherapy trials, pathological complete response occurred in 80 of 260 with low TILs (0% to 10%), 117 of 373 with intermediate TILs (11% to 59%) and 136 of 273 with high TILs (at least 60%): about 31%, 31% and 50%. These categories describe that analysis and are not universal treatment cutoffs.

Fictional area exercise: region A has 4 units of eligible stroma with 0.4 occupied by infiltrate; region B has 1 unit with 0.6 occupied. Pooled occupied area is (0.4 + 0.6)/(4 + 1) = 20%. Averaging the regional percentages without area weighting gives (10% + 60%)/2 = 35%. This arithmetic illustrates the denominator; it does not prescribe a pixel workflow for clinical semiquantitative scoring.

A fictional sTIL estimate of 30% means that the defined mononuclear infiltrate occupies about 30% of eligible stromal area. It does not mean 30% of all cells are lymphocytes or CD8 cells, or that 30% of cancer cells are being killed. Intratumoral TILs, positive-nucleus fractions, cells per square millimetre and bulk immune RNA measure different things. Additional stains change the measurement rather than silently changing its denominator.

Residual-disease recommendations assess the residual tumour bed rather than simply reusing untreated invasive borders. Keep specimen type, site, treatment setting and observer calibration. A high score does not prove tumour-specific recognition, entry into every malignant nest or a permanent hot-tumour state.

To interpret a stromal TIL estimate, retain the block, sampled site, specimen type and treatment setting, then define the eligible stromal region and its exclusions. The output is a continuous estimated percentage of that area occupied by the specified infiltrate. State whether a trained observer or a computational method produced it, with calibration and regional sampling where relevant. Artifacts, sparse stroma, heterogeneity, observer variation and an unrepresentative sample can limit the result. The section uses finite tissue, and measurement reproducibility is a separate question from validation for clinical treatment selection.

TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.

The Loi analysis pooled nine studies. In its node-negative subgroup with at least 30% stromal TILs, three-year overall survival was 99% (95% CI 97% to 100%) after the specified adjuvant chemotherapy. Denkert’s pooled neoadjuvant population contained 3,771 patients overall, including the 906 TNBC patients described above. These population and subgroup findings do not make the study categories universal beneficial-TIL thresholds or establish additional pembrolizumab benefit by score.

In a fictional section, 0.4 square millimetres of mononuclear infiltrate within 2 square millimetres of eligible stroma gives 20% by area. Separately, 30 CD8 cells among 100 counted lymphocytes gives 30% of those counted lymphocytes. Neither is the fraction of all tumour cells, a measure of cancer specificity or evidence of useful killing. One occupied unit among five equal eligible stromal-area units also gives 20%; the drawing illustrates a denominator rather than prescribing pixel counting for semiquantitative breast scoring.

Fixed sections and morphology or selected stains can measure identity, compartment and abundance; viable-cell assays ask about phenotype and function. Dissociation loses native location, culture can select populations and tests consume finite material. Keep cells per square millimetre, specified cell fractions, stromal-area percentages and assay-specific function distinct. TIL therapy is a manufactured expanded-cell product: a tissue count does not establish product yield, composition, potency or treatment success. Sampling, damage, mixed compartments, unsuitable markers and culture selection are different failure modes, and descriptive pathology, research function and clinical treatment selection require different validation.

A UMI is a random sequence tag, rather than a globally unique name. records.tldr: Proteins are amino-acid products that provide structure, catalysis, transport and signaling. A detected fragment and a complete working protein are different findings.

A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

records.name: RNA
records.tldr: RNA is a family of molecules with several jobs. Messenger RNA provides a protein-making template; other RNAs help build, regulate or carry out cellular processes.
records.summary: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

records.name: RNA splicing
records.tldr: RNA processing removes introns and joins retained exons. Different processing choices can produce different messages without changing the underlying gene sequence.
records.summary:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

DNA presence, RNA abundance, intact protein, location and activity require their own evidence. Neither a gene-level RNA count nor a sequence prediction establishes a fixed protein amount or clinical effect.

For a nuclear protein-coding gene in a eukaryotic cell, transcription occurs in the nucleus and the message reaches cytoplasmic ribosomes for translation. A delivered messenger RNA can begin at cytoplasmic translation without requiring genomic integration. This does not imply an empty nucleus or removal of existing nuclear DNA. Neither DNA nor an untranslated message is itself the finished receptor protein. Translation alone does not establish correct folding, processing, transport or function at the cell surface.

In the recipe analogy, the DNA template is retained while an RNA copy is assembled. Translation uses a message as instructions for joining amino acids; the RNA molecule is not the material converted into the protein. The arrows name these processes rather than showing that a reported DNA change produced a measured message or working product. Noncoding RNA lies outside this simplified protein-coding route. Questions about production, location and activity remain open until suitable evidence addresses them.

records.name: DNA
records.tldr: DNA stores sequence information. Its packaging, copying and use as a template for RNA are different processes.
records.summary: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.

records.name: Gene
records.tldr: A gene is a DNA region that produces a functional RNA message. Some messages encode proteins; others work as RNA.
records.summary: A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.

In an invented genomic alignment, position V is retained in two transcripts. In A it falls in the coding sequence; in B a later translation start leaves V in an untranslated region. These are two specified transcript models, not measured abundance, an observed variant effect or proof that both messages yield active proteins. Keep their reference accessions and versions with any consequence claim.

records.name: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
records.tldr: Staining a tissue slice with antibodies so a protein shows up in colour under the microscope.
records.summary: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

notes: There is no universal IHC scoring scale or positivity threshold. Retain antibody clone, retrieval and detection method, controls, eligible cells, subcellular location, intensity, distribution and intended use. A research stain does not automatically replace a clinical selection assay.

An H-score under the intensity-weighted convention is weak-cell percentage plus twice moderate-cell percentage plus three times strong-cell percentage, on a 0 to 300 scale. Fictional example: 50 unstained, 10 weak, 20 moderate and 20 strong cells out of 100 give 50% positive and H-score 110. Neither is a molecule count.

Bulk receptor abundance and staining mainly on blood vessels can both be correct: one measures a mixture and the other locates signal. Neither establishes target accessibility or treatment benefit. Staining also does not establish protein activity or cancer-cell dependence on that protein.

IHC makes selected proteins visible through antibody binding and signal development in a prepared section. Specificity, retrieval, detection, positive controls, internal controls and background matter. Nuclear and membrane signals answer different questions. Multiplex fluorescence adds markers but still needs validated antibody performance and cell-boundary assignment.

In the conventional Allred scheme, proportion categories are 0 for no positive cells, 1 for less than 1%, 2 for 1% to 10%, 3 for 11% to 33%, 4 for 34% to 66% and 5 for 67% to 100%. Intensity is 0 for absent staining or 1, 2 and 3 for weak, moderate and strong staining. The total is 0 or 2 to 8. In a fictional separate example, 30% positive cells with moderate staining give 3 + 2 = 5. These integer bins are a named convention, not a universal positivity rule.

Equal H-scores can conceal different intensity distributions. A negative clinical category does not establish zero protein molecules. HER2 and hormone-receptor assays have marker-specific reporting rules; current CAP breast reporting retains percentage and intensity even when an optional composite score is given.

A useful IHC result identifies the block, fixation and section, antibody clone, retrieval and detection system, eligible cells and scored compartment. Cutting and staining use finite tissue. Report the percentage, intensity, location and named scoring scale, together with expected-positive tissue, relevant internal controls and background assessment. Poor preservation, nonspecific binding, few eligible cells, heterogeneous staining and observer variation can limit interpretation. Validation must fit the assay and its intended use; a research measurement is not automatically a clinical selection test.

Staining recognises an antibody-defined molecular feature, or epitope, rather than automatically proving a complete functioning protein. In an invented repair-gene example, weaker staining in identified cancer cells than in normal neighbours supports a cell-specific signal difference if the controls are adequate. The antibody may recognise a fragment or more than one protein form, so this does not give the amount of intact useful repair protein. The relevant form and current repair need suitable measurements of their own. One validated method can sometimes answer several questions, but measuring one property does not establish every other one.

records.name: Drug target and mechanism of action
records.tldr: A drug target is the molecule or structure a treatment acts on and its mechanism of action is how that action produces an effect, and each step from target to patient benefit needs its own evidence.
records.summary:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

records.tldr: Controlled perturbations deliberately change specified factors and compare responses with suitable controls. A model response alone does not prove its mechanism or patient benefit.
records.summary: A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. Vehicle, positive, negative and mechanism controls answer different questions. A reproducible response can support an experimental claim without establishing its proposed mechanism or patient benefit. Baseline growth, timing, dose and the actual unit assigned to treatment matter.

notes: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

Keep what changed, the comparator, concentration or dose range, timing, assignment, readout and units, sample identities, replicate structure and variability. Repeated wells address variation under their preparation and allocation; independently obtained biological samples address another source of variation. Many wells from one tumour do not become independent patients, and repetition or a small p-value does not repair a missing comparison. A two-drug experiment needs vehicle, both single drugs and the combination. A larger combination effect than either single drug is not automatically synergy; that claim needs a stated reference model.

Fictional direct counts: vehicle-treated cells increase from 100 to 200 while drug-treated cells remain at 100. The endpoint drug count is half the vehicle count without measured net decline from the starting count, so calling it 50 per cent killing overstates the observation. Slower growth, death and a molecular change require their own readouts; direct death or recovery measurements could address further questions. Hafner and colleagues showed that conventional IC50 and maximal-effect measures depend on cell divisions during an assay and developed growth-rate metrics to address that dependence. A real experimental response does not by itself establish the responsible target or clinical benefit.

A fictional two-drug table normalises remaining viability to vehicle at 100 per cent: A leaves 70, B leaves 80, and combination examples leave 56 or 30. Highest single agent uses the better single-drug effect, a 70 per cent remaining-viability reference here. Bliss independence predicts 0.70 times 0.80 = 0.56, or 56 per cent. Both combinations exceed the HSA effect; 56 matches Bliss while 30 exceeds it at that dose pair. A further combination leaving 65 exceeds HSA but not Bliss. Loewe additivity instead needs equivalent-dose information from suitable individual dose-response curves; this one-point table cannot establish it. Report the model, dose-pair pattern, uncertainty and schedule. Interaction relative to a reference does not identify a biological mechanism, tolerable human exposure or a treatment choice.

A rescue restores a proposed missing function or supply and tests whether a defined effect reverses. Adding a cake mix back after its removal implicates the mixture without identifying flour, sugar or another ingredient; likewise, broad mevalonate add-back does not isolate cholesterol. More specific branch perturbations and appropriate add-backs can narrow the explanation. Partial rescue can reflect incomplete delivery or restoration as well as additional contributors, so it does not prove a second cause. Place the add-back relative to the blocked step: supplying GGPP after an upstream synthesis block is different from inhibiting the transferase that uses GGPP, which the added substrate cannot simply be assumed to bypass. Include restoration-only and matched controls, verify the restored process and distinguish growth, morphology and death. A genetic perturbation also has its own specificity limits.

Attribute each readout to the relevant cells. An ATP-based signal can change through cell number or per-cell metabolism, and slower single-cell mass accumulation does not by itself show death. Direct death measurements and regrowth after washout ask further questions; regrowth concerns surviving cells, not revival of cells already dead. A mixed culture can change composition, and a nonmalignant-cell label alone does not establish a validated healthy-tissue control. Ladan's breast-slice chemotherapy assay was compared with response during preoperative treatment in a defined setting. That assay-specific validation does not validate every postoperative combination, human exposure or clinical decision. An inadequate viable preparation should remain uninterpretable rather than be called resistant.

An expression score requires compatible RNA input, locked preprocessing, genes, weights, reference, endpoint/horizon and software version. Existing data can be rescored without new tissue; acquiring RNA consumes material. Report categories, ranks, probabilities or unitless scores on their exact scale. Missing genes, batch, mixture and population shift undermine cutoffs; analytical, clinical and utility evidence remain separate.

An expression-program score has meaning within its algorithm and background. For a score formed by subtracting matched control-gene expression, zero need not mean that no program genes were detected. The 90th percentile places a result relative to a specified reference; it does not mean that 90 percent of cells express the program or that a pathway is 90 percent active. Changing the genes, preprocessing, controls or reference can change the scale, so retain them with the method and version.

records.name: Multi-omic integration
records.tldr: Multi-omic integration analyses measurements from different molecular layers, such as DNA, RNA and protein, side by side while keeping track of what each one measured and which specimen it came from.
records.summary: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

notes: Integration card for combining molecular layers (a reading guide, not a score). Measures: relationships among named layers, not one universal multi-omic score. How: match evidence records, check quality and comparability, harmonise features, compare or model, then evaluate the stated question. Input and tissue cost: existing assay data and metadata; computation uses no extra tissue, but each original assay has its own specimen cost. Output and units: a comparison, factors, clusters or predictions, with the model version and underlying units. Thresholds: specific to the method and validated task, and none applies to every integration. Failure modes: sample swaps, cell-mixture changes, batch confounding, missing data and information leaking into evaluation. Cannot establish alone: causation, malignant-cell target location or better treatment outcomes. Validation tier: research integration gives neither its inputs nor its resulting model a clinical status.

Figure reading (fictional): the same DNA call, a T in the sequence A C T G A, is copied into Report A, Report B and Report C, which is one observation reported three times. A separate RNA assay showing a splice junction is a new measurement that answers a new question, and it does not by itself confirm the DNA call.

Figure reading (fictional Target Q): specimen S at time T1 supplies bulk RNA, where Q is abundant, and a tissue image, where Q protein is seen in normal vessel cells. Whether malignant cells carry accessible Q is unresolved, a model-imputed Q is labelled as an estimate rather than a measurement, and a different specimen or time point is not paired evidence.

Genome, transcriptome and proteome name DNA, RNA and protein collections. An omics profile measures many features within a layer, subject to its coverage and capture limits; it does not necessarily inspect every molecule. Molecular layer and spatial or cellular resolution answer different questions. Multi-omic integration relates the measured layers, with their specimen and analysis context retained, rather than turning a larger number of assays into a universal measure of certainty.

Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

A practical report reading starts with six questions: what specimen, region, date and treatment context were sampled; what object and units were measured with which assay version; whether the result is signed clinical, preliminary, research or model-predicted evidence; which controls or reference support the comparison; what remains unmeasured; and which actual decision could change. A missing field is a question to resolve, not a fact to assume. For fictional pretreatment bulk RNA, high R relative to a stated reference supports captured expression in that mixture. Calling it a surface target remains an interpretation until the contributing cells and accessible protein are established; selectivity, dependence and treatment benefit need their own evidence. Molecular layer and resolution are separate axes. Mapping 500 RNA targets in one section adds location relative to a pooled RNA result, while the measured layer remains RNA. It does not add a membrane-protein or functional measurement. In that invented example, one pretreatment breast-biopsy region contains malignant cells and normal neighbours; no other disease site was sampled. R is reported in the assay's normalised units against a compatible reference, so high belongs to that comparison. Another broad RNA profile need not resolve the missing cell or membrane-protein location. The result can focus research follow-up; treatment selection still needs the validated biomarker-treatment link, clinical setting and eligibility.

An entirely fictional core-biopsy report lists invasive carcinoma of no special type, grade 3; ER and PR below 1 percent; HER2 IHC one-plus; Ki-67 positivity of 60 percent; stromal TILs of 30 percent; PD-L1 22C3 combined positive score 15; and a supported TP53 missense finding at VAF 38 percent on a tumour-only panel. These observations retain separate rules and denominators. The diagnosis describes the sampled region; the receptor results support a triple-negative category and low HER2 staining under the stated testing rules, without establishing a particular drug benefit. Ki-67 positivity is not a treatment-selection rule here. The stromal score is an eligible-area assessment, not proof of recognition, and CPS is its own defined stain score rather than a universal immune percentage. VAF is not inherited status, cancer-cell fraction or measured variant function. KEYNOTE-355 tested pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy in previously untreated advanced TNBC; its CPS-at-least-ten group had median PFS 9.7 versus 5.6 months, hazard ratio 0.65. KEYNOTE-522 enrolled high-risk early TNBC regardless of PD-L1 status. A score cannot transfer benefit between those settings. None of these invented values is a patient observation or a prescription.
